notes.note: Arrangement: Organized as one filing series called POS - WPA; Arrangement: the arrangement is alphabetical by state name, then by artist (with unidentified artists filed as 'anonymous'),  then by assigned sequential number. Call number example: POS - WPA - PA .S56, no. 1 (B size).
Collection title devised by Library staff.
The poster media are predominately silkscreen, lithograph, and woodcut prints.
Special Collections in the Library of Congress / compiled by Annette Melville. Washington, D.C. : Library of Congress, 1980, no. 265
Digitized images of each print along with associated descriptive information are available through the Prints & Photographs Online Catalog.
Digitized images are also available through the Library of Congress, American Memory Web site produced ca. 2002 and called: By the people, for the people, posters from the WPA. Closed in 2013.

The posters resulted from one of the first U.S. government programs to support the arts. They were designed to publicize exhibits, community activities, theatrical productions, and health and educational programs in seventeen states and the District of Columbia, with the strongest representation from California, Illinois, New York, Ohio, and Pennsylvania.
Some published in: Posters of the WPA / Christopher DeNoon. Los Angeles : Wheatley Press, 1987.

item.summary: Includes almost half of the posters created by the United States Works Progress Administration, later Work Projects Administration (WPA). Many posters publicize the Depression-era activities of WPA branches such as the Federal Art Project, Federal Music Project, Federal Theatre Project, and the Index of American Design. These groups produced plays, concerts, dance performances, revues, operas, and art and design exhibitions. Other posters offer health information related to maternity, nutrition, safety sanitation, tuberculosis, syphilis, and cancer. Civic life posters promote travel, museums, libraries, parks, zoos, education, lectures, hobbies, recreation, and employment, including domestic work and issues related to women, children, and youth. Later posters address the war effort and home front activities of World War II, including war bonds, charities, civil liberties, conservation and thrift, trade and productivity, and propaganda. In addition to their value as historic documents, WPA posters are recognized as an artistically significant body of work, innovative both in design and in screen printing techniques.

reproductions:
Generally, Guide Records describe large groups of items from which a selection must be made. The individual items in the group may or may not be represented online.

1. Determine whether the desired materials can be retrieved online.

  • Select the "About this Item" tab and look for a note about tools for searching the group
  • If there is a note such as "Digitized images of most prints along with associated descriptive information are available through the Prints & Photographs Online Catalog," try searching the name of the collection in Search All
  • Select the "Obtaining Copies" tab for any retrieved items that are of interest.

2. If the desired material cannot be retrieved online:

  • A visit to the Prints & Photographs Reading Room may be necessary. You may wish to discuss access to the group of images with reference staff. General information about service in the reading room is available at: http://www.loc.gov/rr/print/info/001_ref.html and contact information is available at: http://www.loc.gov/rr/print/address.html
